title: One-Way Doors
summary:
A **one-way door** is a decision you cannot easily walk back through. The cost of reversing it is not engineering effort in your own code but **other people and stored data depending on it**. The three that matter in system design:

- **API.** Once clients integrate, every field name, meaning, error code and default is a contract. Removing or re-interpreting one breaks someone you cannot redeploy.
- **Data flow.** Who produces which event, who consumes it, and what the message means. Downstream consumers build on it.
- **Data modeling.** How data is shaped, keyed and stored. Migrating billions of rows, or changing the meaning of an ID that is already in URLs and other tables, is slow and risky.

**Hold one-way doors to a very high standard**: review them with consumers, write them down, think about what you will want in two years. Prefer designs that can *grow additively* (new optional fields, new endpoints, new event types) because additive changes do not break existing callers; and when a break is unavoidable, version it and migrate gradually.

Everything else (instance sizes, cache TTLs, internal module boundaries, which queue library) is a [two-way door](#/sd/f/two-way-door): decide quickly, change later. The skill is *sorting decisions* into the right bucket, and spending your scarce care on the first.

drills.q: Which of these are one-way doors? Select all that apply.
options: The name, type and meaning of a field in a public API response
The schema and key design of a table that other services read
The cache eviction policy (LRU vs LFU) of an internal cache
The shape and meaning of an event that three other teams consume
The number of replicas of a stateless service
drills.explain: Public contracts, shared data models and published events all have external dependents. Eviction policy and replica count are internal knobs you can change with a deploy and no one else notices.

drills.q: A public API returns `"price": 12.5` (float, dollars). Two years later the team wants integer cents. Why is this painful, and what would have avoided it?
options: It is not painful: just change the field type in the next deploy
Clients parse the existing field; a silent change breaks them. It needed careful modelling up front, and now needs a versioned or additive change (a new `price_cents` field)
It is painful only because of the database; the API can change freely
It could have been avoided by using GraphQL
drills.explain: The type and unit of a published field is a contract. The tempting 'just change it' breaks every client you cannot redeploy. The remedy is additive evolution (add the new field, deprecate the old, migrate callers).

drills.q: You are unsure whether a new internal service should be one process or two. A team member wants a three-week design review to decide. How should you treat this decision?
options: Spend the three weeks: every architecture decision deserves it
Decide fast and keep the boundary clean, because process layout is a two-way door; spend the review time on the public API instead
Defer all decisions until real traffic arrives
Always choose microservices, since splitting later is impossible
drills.explain: Care should be proportional to irreversibility. Deployment shape is cheap to change when code boundaries are clean; the API that other teams call is not.

drills.q: Order the steps to make a breaking change to a published API without breaking clients.
items: Add the new version or field alongside the old one
Announce deprecation and help clients migrate
Monitor traffic on the old version until it reaches (near) zero
drills.explain: Both versions live side by side so nobody is forced to move at once; removal happens only when telemetry shows nobody depends on the old contract. Removing first and fixing complaints later is how outages are made.

drills.q: Name the three classic one-way doors in system design and give one habit that lowers their risk.
drills.answer: API, data flow, and data modeling. Habit: design them to evolve additively (new optional fields/events instead of changing existing ones), review them with consumers, and version any unavoidable break.
